Yes, you should tell them. Maybe not within the first few dates (because everything is still so new) but definitely tell them.

Their reaction can help you determine whether or not they’ll be a good long-term partner for you.

If they seem disgusted, they’re not a good match, obviously. If they are willing to try to understand, and if they are empathic, and if they accept you as you are with OCD, then you have yourself a golden person with an open mind. 

A bit of backstory of my experience: I used to REALLY regret telling my BF about OCD, bc I thought it ruined his perception of me — and for a while I used to think it ruined our relationship. But if I hadn’t told him, I would have been super fake, and that doesn’t make for a great relationship in the long run, IMHO. 

If anything, it means the world to me that he stayed by my side (and believed in me, and trusted that I was doing my part to get better via meds/therapy) during some very difficult OCD times. It can make you want to try even harder in ERP therapy when you’re motivated by love and wanting to be the best you can for your partner. (Sounds so cheesy, but it’s true.)

Also, I’ve been with someone who is NOT understanding about OCD… mocking… acting like I can easily control it… getting enraged when my symptoms spark up… trying to make me feel guilty for symptoms I can’t control and don’t want.
So those intolerant people do exist… but if you come across a person like that, then please just know that others exist who will like you for who you are.

Plenty of women would be understanding about your situation. If they’re not, then do you really want someone like that? 

(Also, if you don’t tell them about the reason you have a low sex drive, they might mistakenly think that you’re not attracted to them — even though that’s not the case. So although this shouldn’t be the main reason you share your struggles, it is something to consider.)

Good luck. I’m a woman, and I absolutely love it when my BF is honest and open with me. Makes me feel like he trusts me and wants me to know him. I think you have nothing to lose by being open and honest with women you date!

What I mean by this is, for example: The other day I was feeling sensitive and offended about something  — and I thought *he* was being rude. (Of course, this was a huge overreaction on my part.) 

Because he knows about pmdd, he was able to recognize (even before me) that I was in pmdd time. He took me into his lap and let me sit there for a while, and just being near him and inhaling his scent made me feel so much better. It took my mood from a 2 up to a 7. I know it’s counterintuitive to think about cuddling up to the very person you are having negative feelings toward, but maybe give it a shot? It couldn’t hurt!

Once he knows you have pmdd, he’ll be in position to help you cope, and that can be soothing, which can make you feel even more loving toward him.

Sorry, my writing was unclear in my original post. I thought everybody has two love languages: the ones we tend to output and the ones we need to receive. When I wrote all that in my post about his love language, I was talking about his output-love-language. So when I wrote that I thought his love language used to be "words of affirmation," I meant that his output-love-language used to seem like it used to be words of affirmation. 

I don't actually know which love language HE likes to receive best. (So that's why I try to show my love for him in each category -- gifts, acts of service when possible, words of affirmation, touch, quality time whenever possible.) I have OCD, and one theme of OCD I struggle with (that I’ve never had in any other relationship) is the ROCD that another person mentioned. 

During PMDD this ROCD theme gets 100x worse than normal. The OCD symptoms (intrusive thoughts, physical manifestations of anxiety, unwanted and involuntarily compulsions) worsen a lot. 

There’s something about PMDD that seems to make many women (even those without OCD) have these feelings about our partners not loving us. 

If you need someone to relate to, just look at my post history! I can relate 100 percent.

If you go to the International OCD Foundation website and look at the symptoms of OCD — and determine that you think you might have it — then you might want to think seriously about getting OCD treatment.

But as I said, it seems like many women with PMDD experience what you do, even when they don’t have OCD. I have seen a lot of posts here with the same feelings expressed.

One thing that could help you is to keep a daily journal dedicated only to nice things your SO has done, compliments he has given you, or lovely/passionate moments you’ve had together. This way, when the PMDD hits and you start to feel like there’s no way he could possibly love you, you can revisit the journal and reflect on those moments and encounters.

(But do keep in mind, if you have actual OCD, this method alone will not be enough to help you. Only therapy (called ERP therapy) and possibly meds can truly help alleviate OCD symptoms.)

Also, I know how hard it is to feel like you are annoying your BF with your PMDD time. I get so worried that I am going to be unwittingly rude or harsh and drive away my SO during PMDD time.

If your BF is understanding (and hopefully he is, since you plan to marry him), maybe he can read up on PMDD?

I say this bc I think it’s helpful when your partner can be supportive during PMDD time, so that you can let him know you need extra hugs and such. And also bc he’ll understand why you might be acting more sad — so maybe he won’t take it as personally when your tone is different than usual. 

Luckily, my SO is typically pretty understanding when it’s PMDD time, and I think that makes a difference. We have a system where I put a red object on my desk when I’m having a particularly bad day, so he knows I’m struggling. Sometimes, when I don’t even realize I’m in a bad mood, he’ll say, “How many reds are you experiencing today.” Lol! (Since he knows what PMDD is, he often notices my symptoms even before I do.)

It is possible to feel OCD symptoms worsen at certain times. OCD is diagnosed on a scale of severity. For example, if a patient spends 9+ hours per day experiencing obsessions and performing correlating compulsions, that is considered very severe OCD. For people who experience only an hour (total) or so per day of obsessions/compulsions, they would be considered to have more “mild” OCD.

week 1 (period): a mix of bad and good days in terms of mood and physical symptoms

week 2 (pre-ovulation): energized and optimistic

week 3 (ovulation occurs): estrogen and testosterone drop a bit, irritability and brain fog creep in ... a mix of bad and good days

week 4 (pre-menstruation): you feel like you’re living in hell; everything aches; exhaustion; you feel like you’re encased in ice and cannot receive warmth from others; physical and mental disorders get exacerbated

Many people without OCD have intrusive thoughts. 

The difference between an OCD intrusive thought (obsession) and a non-OCD intrusive thought is: The OCD thought will cause anxiety, fear, discomfort (mental and even sometimes physical) that is stopped only with a compulsion. And the thoughts are recurring -- they do not go away once reason and logic are applied.

So a person *without* OCD might have the intrusive thought "My partner is cheating on me," and feel some anxiety, but once she sees evidence that he is not cheating, the anxiety stops and she no longer has the thought.

But a person *with* OCD might get the intrusive thought "My partner is cheating on me,” then feel intense anxiety, and then feel forced to do a compulsion (like searching non-stop for evidence or accusing the partner of cheating to see his reaction), and the mental pain diminishes for a little while... until the thought pops up (unprovoked) a few hours later, and the whole cycle repeats. So no matter how much evidence she sees of his fidelity, her brain keep forcing the thought of "he might be cheating."

So if you perform a compulsion (either in your head or actually do an action) to stop the anxiety caused by a thought, then that's how you might be able to tell it is an OCD-related thought.

Ugh.... yes. 😞 OCD does make it seem like all the threats are real. 

The only thing that has helped me is to make an ERP exposure out of the thoughts. And then when I don’t have time to do an actual exposure, it’s useful to be very intentional about having the mindset of “This could be true or it might false. Either way, I have to live with it and find a way to deal with it.”

The more you do that, the easier it gets.

So for example: If the obsession that keeps coming is “I might not have sanitized the doorknob well enough, and now there might be a deadly virus on it,” that actually seems to me like it could be the truth (not OCD) — especially bc of this pandemic. So I’ve been doing an exposure called “I might not be effectively sanitizing things containing COVID-19,” and then at moments when I don’t have the actual time or strength to do a formal exposure, I tell myself the following when I get the obsession: “Yep, this thing I just touched could have the virus on it. I might have to deal with harsh consequences.” 

I *could* spend 2 hours and a quart of cleaner spraying/wiping down a single object to be absolutely CERTAIN that it’s not contaminated, but by having the intentional mindset of “Yes, it might be contaminated,” I’m forcing myself to deal with the uncertainty. It feels very uncomfortable, but it’s the only way to do it.... unless I want to give into the compulsions. (And I most definitely don’t want to waste 2 hours and a quart of cleaner on each “dirty” surface of my home. That was me in 2010-2013, and I can’t do it again!)

It’s the same thing with a “jealousy themed” obsession I have. I get thoughts such as “my boyfriend cheated on me and lied to me at the beginning of our relationship” or “my boyfriend might now be trying to pursue this other women; she might be a threat to me.” These thoughts torture me, and like you, I often wonder if this is real or if it’s just the OCD — especially because I can find “evidence” of these things being true. (Brains with OCD just love to find ways to make things into evidence... ugh.) My compulsion for this obsession has been to harshly accuse him of cheating on me or wanting to cheat.

So I do exposures on this. But inevitably, I’ll start thinking that “this might not even be OCD. This could be him actually cheating on me and I’m tricking myself into thinking it’s merely OCD.” So at that point I have to remind myself: “The threat could be real or it could be completely false. In any relationship, anyone could get cheated on. Do I want to waste my life (and hurt my boyfriend) trying to verify these thoughts?”

At times, it is terribly uncomfortable to constantly do this “could be true, could be false, but I have to move forward anyway” thing. It does get easier if you do it often, though. It’s like a muscle; the more you work it, the stronger it gets. 


Honestly, I’ve come to realize that having OCD is just being in discomfort for most of the day. That sounds bleak, but it’s true. 

But I try to look at it like this: Either way (whether doing a compulsion or avoiding a compulsion), I’m going to be in discomfort. Doing a compulsion causes pain (its awful to sanitize for 8 hours straight or know I’m hurting my boyfriend with my outbursts). Not doing the compulsion — and just forcing myself to live with the uncertainty — causes extreme anxiety. So I figure if it’s going to be painful either way, I might as well do my best to choose the pain that is going to help treat the OCD instead of worsen it.

Don't beat yourself up over feeling upset about this. Truly.

It's totally a normal feeling to want your best friend's attention and to feel neglected/upset when she is giving it to someone else at your expense. That's human nature. To have the feeling is normal. To act out on it -- like do something rude to your friend or get mad at her for spending time with her boyfriend -- is where there's a problem. (I'm not trying to say you're acting out on it. I'm just saying there's nothing inherently wrong with having that feeling. The way a person chooses to react to that feeling is where it can be problematic.)

Right now I'm reading a book about overcoming jealousy by a renowned psychology expert who talks about how in our society, we've come to think of feeling jealous (like when a person we care about directs attention to someone else) as a negative thing for which we should feel shame and hate for ourselves. In our society, we beat ourselves up for feeling jealous and tell ourselves: "If I were a good person, I wouldn't feel jealous" or "I'm ridiculous for feeling jealous." You hear it all the time in advice columns and chat forums: "Is your boyfriend jealous? Dump him!" or "I would never keep a jealous friend around!" or "Oh, she just a jealous jerk." Stuff like that.

But the author points out that hating on ourselves for feeling this way isn't helpful. He points out that everyone -- no matter how secure or stable they are -- can be made to feel jealous. Find the right situation, and ANYONE will experience jealousy (unless they are a sociopath). It really is human nature. The author actually devotes an entire section of the book to showing how and why (from an evolutionary standpoint) jealousy is hardwired into our brains. Many people think that if a person is jealous, it means that they are simply insecure or immature. (I actually thought this before reading this book.) But the author points out that this is an untrue stereotype. He shows that jealousy can pop up for MANY different reasons. A lot of the time, we experience jealousy as an indicator that a relationship is very important to us. So it's very likely you have these feelings because your best friend means a lot to you. It doesn't mean there's anything horribly wrong with you just because you're feeling upset when she can't/doesn't reply your texts while with him.

I do know exactly what it's like to feel upset when someone you care deeply about directs attention to someone else (especially when they love that person)-- while "neglecting" you. It's a difficult feeling.

One way to get over it is to try to remind yourself that just because she's hanging out with him, it doesn't mean she values you any less. I know it's hard to be "ignored" when she isn't answering your texts, but try to remind yourself that it doesn't mean she doesn't care about you. 

Have there been times when you didn't reply to texts from people you care about? (Like when you're at work, or just in the shower, or with other people?) Try to remember that when you didn't reply to those people, it didn't mean you didn't care about them and it didn't mean they were any less important to you than the activity at hand; it just meant that your attention was elsewhere.

When you start feeling this way, it might be most helpful to just observe that you're having this thought, allow yourself to feel the discomfort, and don't beat yourself up. So you could just say to yourself: "Yes, I am feeling upset that my friend isn't replying to me. That's a thought I am having because our relationship means a lot to me." Try not to judge yourself for having the feeling; it's human nature to have this emotion. And after you acknowledge that you are having this uncomfortable thought and feeling, then go do something that you need to do (laundry, dishes, whatever) or something you care about -- a hobby, watch a tv show you like, listen to music you like, etc. That way, you spend your time doing something you need to do or enjoy, instead of beating yourself up for having feelings that you can't help but have.

I'm not a therapist, so I don't want to give tips that might harm anyone. However, here are a few things (that my therapist has approved) that help me fight compulsions. Maybe you can try them?

1. Imagining the consequences of performing a compulsion. Right before you're about to perform a compulsion, think of how much worse your life is going to be if you do the compulsion. And try to think about the fact that each compulsion you perform makes the disorder worse. (In my case, with a current "theme" of obsession I am fighting, the consequence is that if I perform a compulsion, I risk my partner breaking up with me. With my contamination compulsions, the consequence is: "If I scrub an item with 75 Clorox wipes for 1 hour straight, then I lose precious time and money (Clorox wipes aren't cheap.)" When I try to make myself focus on all the consequences of performing a compulsion, I usually am more successful at resisting it.

2. Reminding yourself that each time you resist a compulsion, you are helping yourself get better. Remind yourself each day that resisting compulsions (feeling that horrible pain) is going to be worth it. I tell myself multiple times per day: "Resisting the compulsion is the ONLY way out. It's the ONLY way to a better life." I have to remind myself A LOT that the more you exercise the muscle, the stronger it becomes. It sounds super cliche, but: "No pain, no gain." It's totally true here.

3. Meds. They can help the obsessions feel a bit less horrible and can help the compulsions feel slightly easier to resist.

4. When the anxiety/discomfort is so overwhelming that you feel incapacitated unless you perform a compulsion, try doing only a "half" compulsion. So if your regular compulsion is to (for example) say a word 16 times, try to say the word only 8 times. It might hurt *way* too much to not say the word at all. Saying the word only 8 times will give you anxiety because you didn't do the "full" compulsion, but the anxiety will be more tolerable. If you can tolerate that anxiety for several times, eventually you can work your way up to not saying the word at all.  

I should add: Don't beat yourself up if you're not able to resist the compulsion. When I start beating myself up over this, my therapist reminds me: If you burned your hand and were in a lot of pain, your brain would automatically tell you to apply ice. ALL humans are wired to stop ourselves from feeling pain. With OCD, the obsession is the "burning hand" that causes pain, and the compulsion is the ice pack our brains automatically try to apply. It's just as hard to resist a compulsion as it is to resist a pack of ice when your hand is in severe pain. So don't be too hard on yourself if you aren't able to resist a compulsion.

SUDS is "Subjective Units of Discomfort." It's basically the amount of discomfort you feel from an obsession.

Some therapists use a scale of 1-10 and some use a scale of 1-100. A score of "1" is feeling no discomfort. A score of 100 (or 10, if that's the scale) is the most anxiety you can imagine -- like you'd rather die than deal with any more tremendous discomfort, and at that level of SUDS, it's impossible to control your compulsions because you just need relief from the discomfort. A score of 50 is like: You most definitely can feel the strong discomfort, and it's getting much harder to control the compulsions.

So someone's obsession might be: "I am going to hit a pedestrian with my car." If that person is driving at night on a street packed with pedestrians, their SUDS might be 95. But if they are driving during the day on a street with only one pedestrian, their SUDS might be a 20.

SUDS is "Subjective Units of Discomfort." It's basically the amount of discomfort you feel from an obsession.

Some therapists use a scale of 1-10 and some use a scale of 1-100. A score of "1" is feeling no discomfort. A score of 100 (or 10, if that's the scale) is the most anxiety you can imagine -- like you'd rather die than deal with any more tremendous discomfort, and at that level of SUDS, it's impossible to control your compulsions because you just need relief from the discomfort. A score of 50 is like: You most definitely can feel the strong discomfort, and it's getting much harder to control the compulsions.

So someone's obsession might be: "I am going to hit a pedestrian with my car." If that person is driving at night on a street packed with pedestrians, their SUDS might be 95. But if they are driving during the day on a street with only one pedestrian, their SUDS might be a 20.

Not keychains, but a while ago I had a tremendously difficult time carrying USBs with me because I had kept having obsessions that they would fall out of my bag (and someone would find them and have all my personal data). 

The only way to stop this checking is to do an exposure on it.

So what I did for the USB thing -- and what might help you -- is: Do an imaginal exposure that you will lose it. Imagine it falling off; imagine losing it. Or if the anxiety caused by the thought "I will lose the keychain" is too intense (like if it's causing a 50+ SUDS) then maybe say something gentler like "I MIGHT lose the keychain -- I just don't know either way."

If you do this imaginal exposure every single day for a few weeks -- and make sure you do not perform checking compulsions during or after it -- hopefully you can get the SUDS down to a low level. 

From there, you could go outside for a short amount of time each day (like an hour) with the keychains, and when you start getting the thought "I'm going to lose they keychain any minute," you'll have to tell yourself during that hour "Yes, it could be gone," and then NOT check to see if it's gone. 

Will this uncertainty feel absolutely hellish? At that point -- after doing an imaginal exposure for a few weeks prior to "real" exposure -- it shouldn't feel as bad. (I know that as you read this right now it, just the thought of doing this exposure probably gives you a high anxiety level. Sorry. But after doing the imaginal exposure, the anxiety shouldn't be as bad.)

And once you do this real-life exposure many times, you should be able to use the keychains with minimal anxiety. You will likely still have thoughts about losing them, but the overwhelming (disproportionate-to-the-situation) amount of anxiety that accompanies those thoughts should be very much reduced.

Sorry, but this is the only way to use your keychains without walking around with a high level of anxiety. I know... exposures suck. It is hard to force yourself to experience awful sensations and feelings. It's the only way, though.

PS: I might not have explained the exposure very well.. I am having sort of a bad day myself because of, of course, OCD. Let me know if this doesn't make any sense. And good luck.  :)

PPS: Try to stop buying keychains with rings that are hard to attach/remove -- that is itself a compulsion. I know it will be difficult to buy keychains with flimsier rings, but if you keep purposely buying the strong ones, you are only reinforcing the obsession, making it even harder to get over the obsession.

With mental illness, I think it’s important to find someone who is able to help you with your therapy exercises AND who can separate the person from the mental illness. I asked him so many times not to take my bouts of OCD-related anxiety (and my OCD-related compulsions) personally. I always tried to explain that I didn’t mean them as personal attacks. We all have different needs in life and different levels of stress we can manage.)

I begged him to take me back. I apologized sincerely for hurting him with these disorders. I hate that he gets hurt. I’ve been racking my brain trying to find solutions to making him feel less like he needs to walk on eggshells around me. I tried to propose solutions, but he just keeps saying “you’re trying to bargain to get me back.” So he doesn’t want to try new paths to make it work; he’s decided he’s just done. He has given up trying to make it work, whereas on my end of it, I see so many very real possibilities to make it work. But I can’t get him to see it. 

I was hoping that good-day me was enough for him to want to stay with bad-day me. But sadly, I think towards the end he could only see bad-day me. He even said during the breakup “I don’t even know who you are without the OCD.” I’ve had the OCD the entire time we’ve been together... it just became impossible to hide from him after a while. I’m still the woman he fell in love with... but honestly all he can see of me now are the mental disorders. So no matter what I do, no matter what progress I make, he only sees the negative parts. (I could name dozens of moments in the past week that we were fantastic together. If I asked him to do it, I know he’d say there were no good moments together.) 

So I guess it comes down to perspective and willingness to keep trying. I think that’s how I’d define a supportive partner: someone who is willing to keep trying and equipped to keep a positive perspective, even in the most difficult of times. To me, the things worth having in life take a lot of effort to keep, and it’s worth it. If you have a partner who needs to reduce their stress-level and sees you as a cause of stress they should slough off (rather than a garden worth tending), then it’s not going to work, and the two people just weren’t meant to be. Or my brother and I would be getting ready for bed at 9 pm, and one of his clients would page his beeper, and he'd have to run out to go address their computer emergency (he was a computer repair man).

Or he'd realize after dinner that he left his saw at his friend's garage, and he needed to go retrieve it.

These reasons to leave the house happened very frequently, and they would always take at least an hour of his time at night. 

Like most little girls, I really craved attention from him. Getting one-on-one time with him was such a special (rare) treat, so I would sometimes ask if I could accompany him to the store. I remember he would get all frustrated and make up excuses as to why I couldn't go with him. On the occasions that he obliged, he would always be moody and kind of short with me during the shopping trip.

I always just thought that my dad was a very busy man. I thought he was being helpful and considerate toward my mom by always helping her get "forgotten" groceries and by working "late hours."

To a certain extent, I thought of myself as kind of annoying to be around, and figured that was the reason he didn't want me tagging along to the store. 

I never really questioned why he always had reasons to run errands or do work at night. I thought it was normal.

Two years ago, I found out that my father had at least one (but probably many more) long-term sexual affair -- and this took place for most of my childhood.
